checks.prompt: A company has one index over its product documentation, and every user question is a single lookup against it. A second company has three indexes — annual filings, support tickets, product docs — plus a calculator, and its users ask things like 'which of the last two filings showed faster revenue growth?'. Which company should put an agent in front of retrieval, and what exactly is the agent buying?
checks.explanation: A plain query engine is a fixed pipeline: embed, retrieve, stuff, answer. That is exactly right when every question is one lookup — cheap, fast, predictable. What the agent adds is a decision: which source, how many times, and mixed with non-retrieval tools. That is what a multi-hop comparison needs, and it is worth its cost only when questions genuinely branch or chain. An agent with one tool is not free either: it is an extra model call and a chance to choose wrongly.
options: The second. The agent buys routing and chaining: it decides which source to query and can perform several retrievals plus arithmetic on one question, which a fixed retrieve-then-answer pipeline cannot. The first company should stay with the plain query engine, because an agent adds a model-driven control loop — latency, cost and the chance of a wrong tool choice — for agency it never uses

The first. An agent's value is making a single lookup more reliable by re-querying when the retrieved chunks look weak; the second company's comparison question should be handled by a larger index containing all three sources
Both. Agency is strictly additive: an agent given one tool behaves identically to calling that tool directly, so there is no cost to adopting it early
Neither. Comparing two filings requires a purpose-built pipeline, and routing between sources should be written as explicit code rather than left to a model

checks.prompt: Explain this framework's agents with the switchboard analogy, saying what corresponds to the operator, the phone book and an individual entry. Explain what is distinctive about one particular kind of entry, and why that is the framework's defining feature rather than a convenience. Then describe the two runtimes that implement the loop, what differs between them and what does not, and when you would choose each.
checks.expected: A correct answer must build the analogy. A plain retrieval pipeline is a single hard-wired phone line: every question rings the same desk. The agent is the switchboard operator — a model that reads the request, picks an entry from a directory, places the call, reads the answer and decides whether to call again or report back. The phone book is the tool set, and each entry is a tool described by a name, a description and an argument schema. The distinctive entry must be identified: an entire retrieval pipeline can itself be a tool, so querying your data becomes something the agent CHOOSES to do rather than a fixed first step. The answer must say why that is defining rather than cosmetic: it converts static retrieval into dynamic retrieval — several indexes can sit side by side, the model routes each sub-question to the right one, and retrieval mixes freely with arithmetic, code or API calls, none of which a fixed pipeline can express. The two runtimes must be distinguished: one uses the model's native structured tool-calling interface, which is robust and the default where the model supports it; the other uses the text-based reason-act prompt with reasoning, action and observation in plain text, which is the fallback for models without native tool calling and useful when you want the reasoning trace as text. What differs is only the transport — how the tool call is expressed and parsed — while the loop, the tools, the memory and the orchestration are shared. Noting that a conversation context object carries state across turns so follow-up questions remember earlier ones is a plus.

checks.prompt: An agent with five tools keeps calling the wrong one and passing wrong arguments. The tools are ordinary Python functions registered with the framework's helper; two of them have no docstring, three have untyped arguments, and two of the retrieval tools are described as 'search the docs' and 'search documentation'. What is the mechanism behind the failures, and which changes actually address it?
checks.explanation: The tool helper derives everything the model sees from your code: the name from the function, the description from its docstring, and the argument schema from its type hints. That trio is the entire basis for routing, so an undocumented, untyped function is a tool the model cannot reason about, and two tools whose descriptions say the same thing make the choice a coin flip. The fixes are editorial as much as technical — treat the docstring as the tool's prompt, type the arguments, and keep the action space small with non-overlapping purposes.
options: The model routes purely on each tool's name, description and generated argument schema — which the helper derives from the function name, its docstring and its type hints. So a missing docstring gives it nothing to decide with, untyped arguments give it no schema to fill in correctly, and two near-identical descriptions make the choice between them arbitrary. Write the docstring as the tool's prompt, add real type hints, and give the two retrieval tools sharp non-overlapping descriptions — or merge them
The framework inspects the function body to decide relevance, so docstrings are documentation only; the real fix is reordering the tool list so the most-used tools come first
Wrong arguments mean the schema was generated but not passed to the model, which happens only with the text-based runtime; switching runtimes fixes both problems without touching the functions
Five tools is below any routing threshold, so the failures must come from the model's temperature; setting it to zero makes selection deterministic and correct

checks.prompt: Implement the tool layer and the dispatch loop. Write `tool_from(fn, name=None, description=None)` returning `{"name", "description", "parameters", "required", "call"}`: the name defaults to the function's own; the description defaults to the FIRST line of its docstring, or `""` when it has none; `parameters` maps each argument name to a schema type derived from its annotation — `int`→`"integer"`, `str`→`"string"`, `float`→`"number"`, `bool`→`"boolean"`, and `"string"` for anything unannotated; `required` lists, in order, the arguments with no default; and `call` is the function. Write `query_engine_tool(engine, name, description)`, which exposes a retrieval pipeline — any callable taking one question string — as a tool with the single required argument `query`. Write `catalog(tools)`, mapping a name-keyed dict of tools to a list of `{"name", "description", "parameters", "required"}` dicts. Write `run_agent(planner, tools, max_steps=6)`: keep a `state` dict and a `trace` list; each turn call `planner(state, catalog(tools))`, which returns either `{"final": ...}` — return `{"answer": <it>, "steps": <1-based turn>, "trace": trace}` — or `{"tool": name, "args": {...}}` with an optional `"save_as"` key. Dispatch that call, producing an observation: `"Error: unknown tool 'x'. Available: <sorted names, comma-separated>"`; or `"Error: <name> is missing required argument(s): <comma-separated>"`; or `"Error: <name> got unexpected argument(s): <comma-separated>"`; or `"Error: <the exception>"` if the call raises; otherwise the return value. Append `{"tool", "args", "observation"}` to the trace and store the observation in `state` under `save_as`, defaulting to `"step<N>"`. After `max_steps` turns with no final answer return the same shape with `"answer": None`. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The first block is the point of the tool helper: everything the model will use to decide — the name, the description, the argument schema and which arguments are optional — is read straight off your code. The undocumented, untyped function immediately after it is the same mechanism showing you the failure: a tool with an empty description and every argument typed as a string is one the model has nothing to route on. The retrieval tool is the framework's signature move made concrete — a whole pipeline reduced to one tool with a single query argument, which is what lets the agent decide when and where to search instead of always searching first. And the dispatch block is about survivability: a missing argument, an extra argument, a tool that does not exist and a tool that raises all become observations the planner reads and corrects from, while the step cap stops an agent that never concludes.
checks.test:
def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Multiply two integers and return the product.

    Longer prose the model does not need on the first line.
    """
    return a * b


def lookup_capital(country: str, upper: bool = False) -> str:
    """Return the capital city of a given country name."""
    capitals = {"france": "Paris", "japan": "Tokyo"}
    found = capitals.get(country.strip().lower(), f"unknown ({country})")
    return found.upper() if upper else found


mul = tool_from(multiply)
cap = tool_from(lookup_capital)

# What the model is given is derived from the code: the name, the first line of the
# docstring, and a schema read off the type hints.
assert mul["name"] == "multiply", mul
assert mul["description"] == "Multiply two integers and return the product.", mul
assert mul["parameters"] == {"a": "integer", "b": "integer"}, mul
assert mul["required"] == ["a", "b"], mul
assert cap["parameters"] == {"country": "string", "upper": "boolean"}, cap
# An argument with a default is optional, so the model may leave it out.
assert cap["required"] == ["country"], cap
assert mul["call"](a=6, b=7) == 42

# The failure the notebook warns about, made visible: no docstring and no hints
# leave the model with a name and nothing else to route on.
def helper(x, y=1):
    return x


bare = tool_from(helper)
assert bare["description"] == "", bare
assert bare["parameters"] == {"x": "string", "y": "string"}, bare
assert bare["required"] == ["x"], bare

# The name and description can be overridden, which is how the same callable is
# exposed differently to different agents.
renamed = tool_from(multiply, name="product", description="Multiply. Use for maths.")
assert renamed["name"] == "product" and "maths" in renamed["description"]

# The defining move: an entire retrieval pipeline is exposed as one tool, with a
# single query argument -- so the agent DECIDES when to search which source.
def filings_engine(question):
    return f"[10-K] answer to {question!r}"


filings = query_engine_tool(filings_engine, "company_filings",
                            "Search the company's 10-K filings.")
assert filings["parameters"] == {"query": "string"}, filings
assert filings["required"] == ["query"], filings
assert filings["name"] == "company_filings"
assert filings["call"](query="revenue") == "[10-K] answer to 'revenue'"

tools = {t["name"]: t for t in (mul, cap, filings)}


# Two tools chained on one question -- the thing a single fixed pipeline cannot do.
def planner(state, seen):
    assert {entry["name"] for entry in seen} == {"multiply", "lookup_capital",
                                                 "company_filings"}, seen
    if "capital" not in state:
        return {"tool": "lookup_capital", "args": {"country": "France"},
                "save_as": "capital"}
    if "answer" not in state:
        return {"tool": "multiply", "args": {"a": 3, "b": len(state["capital"])},
                "save_as": "answer"}
    return {"final": f"3 x {len(state['capital'])} = {state['answer']}"}


run = run_agent(planner, tools)
assert run["answer"] == "3 x 5 = 15", run
assert run["steps"] == 3, run
assert [entry["tool"] for entry in run["trace"]] == ["lookup_capital", "multiply"], run

# Routing is done off the catalogue, so the description must be there to route on.
seen_catalog = []
run_agent(lambda state, seen: seen_catalog.append(seen) or {"final": "x"}, tools)
assert seen_catalog[0][0]["description"] != "", seen_catalog[0]

# A bad call is an observation the planner can read and correct from, not a crash.
def forgetful(state, seen):
    if "step1" not in state:
        return {"tool": "multiply", "args": {"a": 3}}
    if "step2" not in state:
        return {"tool": "multiply", "args": {"a": 3, "b": 4, "c": 5}}
    if "step3" not in state:
        return {"tool": "search_web", "args": {"q": "x"}}
    return {"final": "recovered"}


run = run_agent(forgetful, tools, max_steps=6)
assert "missing required argument(s): b" in run["trace"][0]["observation"], run["trace"]
assert "unexpected argument(s): c" in run["trace"][1]["observation"], run["trace"]
assert "unknown tool 'search_web'" in run["trace"][2]["observation"], run["trace"]
assert "company_filings" in run["trace"][2]["observation"], run["trace"]
assert run["answer"] == "recovered", run


# A tool that raises is reported the same way rather than ending the run.
def explodes(text: str) -> str:
    """Always fails."""
    raise RuntimeError("no index loaded")


tools["broken"] = tool_from(explodes)
run = run_agent(lambda state, seen: {"tool": "broken", "args": {"text": "x"}}
                if not state else {"final": "ok"}, tools)
assert "no index loaded" in run["trace"][0]["observation"], run
assert run["answer"] == "ok", run

# The loop is bounded: an agent that never concludes is stopped and says so.
run = run_agent(lambda state, seen: {"tool": "multiply", "args": {"a": 1, "b": 1}},
                tools, max_steps=3)
assert run["answer"] is None and run["steps"] == 3, run
assert len(run["trace"]) == 3, run

checks.prompt: A team installs the framework's core package, writes an agent, calls its run method, logs the result and sees nothing happen — no tool calls, no error. They fix that and then hit an import error naming a package they did not install. They also find a blog post whose agent classes do not exist in their version. What are the three explanations?
checks.explanation: Three separate traps that arrive in exactly this order. Runs are asynchronous, so an unawaited coroutine does nothing at all and reports nothing — the quietest failure in the list. The package layout is deliberately split: the core has the agents, tools and workflows but no model, so an integration package for the provider you use is a separate install. And the agent API has been through more than one generation, so class names in older material may simply not exist in the release you installed.
options: Runs are coroutines, so calling the method without awaiting it silently does nothing — use the event loop, or await it in a notebook. The import error is the split-package layout: the core package contains no model, so a model integration package must be installed alongside it. And the agent API has moved through generations, so a tutorial's class names may belong to a superseded one — pin a version and read the documentation for that release

Nothing happening means no tools were registered, which is silent by design; the import error means the core package version is too new for the integration; and the blog post's classes were removed for security reasons and have no replacement
All three are the same problem: the metapackage was not installed, and it supplies the event loop, the model and the current agent classes together
Nothing happening is the step cap defaulting to zero; the import error is an optional dependency that can be ignored; and the differing class names are aliases that resolve at runtime

checks.prompt: You are advising on three systems. (a) A support bot answering from one FAQ index, where latency and predictability matter most. (b) An analyst assistant reasoning across four internal corpora plus a live pricing API, where getting the routing right is most of the value. (c) A long-running operations agent that must keep durable state across sessions, branch on classification results and pause for human approval, with retrieval a minor detail. Recommend for each and justify. Then say what you would need to be true before adding a fifth and sixth retrieval tool to system (b).
checks.expected: A correct answer must place all three with reasons. (a) A plain query engine, not an agent: every question is a single lookup, so the model-driven control loop adds latency, cost and the possibility of a wrong tool choice while buying nothing — the rule is not to pay for agency you do not use. (b) This framework's agents: the job is reasoning over your own data across several sources, which is exactly where wrapping each retrieval pipeline as a tool pays, letting the model route per question and mix retrieval with a live API call; the trade-off worth naming is that the agent API has churned across generations, so versions should be pinned. (c) A graph-based agent runtime, because durable state, explicit branching and human-in-the-loop approval are its subject matter and the data layer is incidental here; the answer should note the cost is more manual wiring and weaker retrieval ergonomics. The final question must be answered as a condition rather than a yes or no: adding tools is safe only if each new one has a sharp, non-overlapping description and a clear argument schema, because routing degrades when descriptions blur — several near-identical retrieval tools make selection unreliable, so the prerequisite is that the corpora are genuinely distinguishable in one sentence, and if they are not the right move is to merge the indexes or route with explicit code rather than adding a sixth fuzzy option. Noting that a step or cost ceiling matters more as the tool set grows, since each retrieval tool can itself be expensive, is a plus.
